text.title: Multi-Platform Design Parity Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for the parity matrix: parity declared as invariant plus allowed variance, tokens generated to platform primitives from one source, no-native-equivalent cells resolved rather than left blank, density tiers with base units, typed and expiring overrides, and a parity score with a published denominator.

rule.statement: Each matrix row MUST declare what is held constant across surfaces (user outcome, information hierarchy, terminology, token semantics) and what is explicitly permitted to differ (control affordance, navigation pattern, motion, gesture). A row with no stated variance allowance defaults to must-match, and any observed difference is a `drift_log` entry.

rationale.source: Apple Human Interface Guidelines and Material Design platform-convention guidance

rule.rationale: When the invariant is never stated, it is settled per pull request by whoever implements last on each surface. The result is an iOS tab bar and an Android bottom nav built to different information hierarchies — each individually idiomatic, jointly a different product, and unfixable without a rewrite on one side.

rule.statement: `token_map` MUST state, per token tier, the concrete output primitive for every surface — CSS custom properties for web, asset catalog or Swift constants for iOS, `colors.xml` or a Compose theme for Android — all generated from a single source (W3C DTCG JSON via Style Dictionary or equivalent). A token with no named primitive on a listed surface is an unresolved cell, not parity.

rationale.source: W3C Design Tokens Format Module + Style Dictionary multi-platform build

rule.rationale: Hand-maintained per-platform token files diverge at the first hotfix shipped on one platform only, and the divergence is silent because each file is internally consistent. Generation makes the same divergence a build failure at the moment it is introduced instead of a discovery two quarters later during an audit.

rule.statement: Every cell where a gesture, control, or density tier has no native equivalent — hover on touch, long-press on web, swipe-to-delete on a remote-control surface, text entry on a wearable — MUST carry either a named substitute interaction plus its discoverability affordance, or an explicit "not offered on this surface" with the reason. Empty cells fail the rule.

rationale.source: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures and SC 2.1.1 Keyboard

rule.rationale: Hover-only and path-gesture-only affordances have no equivalent on touch or D-pad, so a blank cell means the implementer invents one per screen — and the invented substitute is almost always undiscoverable, because discoverability is the part that requires design, not code. The function ships and measures as zero usage.

rule.statement: `density_tiers` MUST name each tier with its base spacing unit, its scale factor, and the surfaces mapped to it — for example a touch tier on an 8dp grid with a 48dp minimum row height, a compact desktop tier for data tables, a 10-foot tier with its own minimum type size and focus-ring weight. A listed surface with no tier mapping is a `drift_log` entry.

rationale.source: Material Design density guidance and Google TV / 10-foot UI design guidance

rule.rationale: Density is the token dimension that does not survive a copy across surfaces: web touch spacing rendered on a TV at three metres produces unreadable type and rows a D-pad cannot traverse efficiently. Because the values still resolve and the build still passes, the failure is only found by someone actually sitting in front of the surface.

rule.statement: Each entry in `platform_overrides` MUST carry a type: platform-convention (system back gesture, share sheet, native date picker — permanent by design), capability-gap (the surface cannot do it), or implementation-gap (temporary). Implementation-gap entries MUST carry an expiry release; without one they are recorded as drift, not as overrides.

rationale.source: Internal — parity audits across web/iOS/Android surfaces

rule.rationale: "Android will catch up next quarter" and "Android follows the platform convention here" are written identically and become indistinguishable within two quarters, once the person who knew the difference has moved on. The type field is what lets a later audit compute a real score instead of counting every deliberate platform difference as a defect.

rule.statement: `parity_score` MUST be published with its formula and cell counts: matching cells divided by cells declared must-match, with platform-convention and capability-gap overrides excluded from the denominator and implementation-gap overrides counted as failures. A score reported without formula and counts is rejected.

rationale.source: Operational definition of a measurement (W. Edwards Deming)

rule.rationale: Two audits of the same product return 68% and 91% purely because one counted convention overrides as failures. An undefined score is unfalsifiable, and an unfalsifiable score ends the parity conversation instead of directing it — which leaves the product worse off than reporting no score at all.

rule.statement: Do NOT apply when the product ships on exactly one surface, when the surfaces are deliberately different products with different information architecture (marketing site versus operator console), or when there is no shared token source and no plan to build one. In the last case run cross-platform-token-distribution first — a parity matrix over hand-maintained token files records drift it cannot prevent.

rationale.source: W3C Design Tokens Format Module + Style Dictionary multi-platform build

rule.rationale: The matrix is an instrument over a generated pipeline: it detects divergence because the generator makes divergence detectable. Without a shared source the matrix has no mechanism behind it and degrades into a manually updated spreadsheet, which drifts faster than the surfaces it describes.
